analysis.one_liner: Requires approved oil spill response plans and full environmental review before offshore drilling permits.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its initial committee referrals, drawing no cosponsors and no floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Written after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster, this bill would tighten federal control over offshore oil drilling. Companies would need an oil spill response plan approved by the Coast Guard's department before getting a drilling permit, drilling exploration plans could no longer skip full environmental review, worst-case spill plans would have to cover uncontrolled well blowouts, and federal water-quality testing would have to start within 48 hours of any reported spill. It also set clearer command structure for who leads a major spill response.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, Gulf Coast communities, fishermen, and tourism businesses that bear the damage when a well blows out. Ordinary people also benefit as taxpayers, since federal law makes spill cleanup costs recoverable and major spills have historically cost the public billions. The bill front-loads prevention requirements so companies prove spill readiness before drilling, not after.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Interior Department from issuing any offshore exploration or production permit unless an oil spill response plan for that facility has been approved under Clean Water Act standards.
Prohibits exploration plans from receiving a categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act, meaning drilling plans could no longer bypass full environmental review.
Requires worst-case discharge plans for vessels and facilities to cover uncontrolled or uncontained well discharges, the failure mode that sank the Deepwater Horizon rig.
Requires EPA water-quality monitoring of affected waters to begin within 48 hours of a reported oil or hazardous substance discharge.

Designates the Coast Guard Commandant as National Incident Commander for major spill responses and requires the National Contingency Plan to be updated at least every five years with separate land and water response plans.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would face a new Coast Guard-approved permit precondition, a longer exploration plan review window (90 days, extendable to 150), and the end of the shortcut that let drilling plans skip full environmental study. Consumers could see some of those compliance and delay costs passed through in energy prices.

drawbacks.text: Extending the exploration plan review deadline from 30 days to 90, with a possible 60-day extension, would slow offshore permitting and could reduce domestic oil production.

The bill adds new regulatory layers and approval requirements, and paperwork requirements like an approved response plan do not by themselves guarantee a company can actually contain a blown-out well in deep water.
The bill gathered no cosponsors, including from other Gulf Coast members, suggesting little appetite even among coastal-state representatives for this specific package.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address a real, demonstrated risk: a single deepwater blowout devastated Gulf fishing and tourism for years and produced the largest marine oil spill in U.S. history. The cost is slower, more expensive permitting for offshore drilling and no guarantee that response plans reflect real containment capability. A serious package, but one that never earned enough support to be tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2011 and split across three subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. C.W. Bill Young (R-FL) introduced the SAFEGUARDS Act of 2011 on April 15, 2011.
The House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure and Natural Resources Committees on the day of introduction.
Within three days it was further referred to three subcommittees: Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, Water Resources and Environment, and Energy and Mineral Resources.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill received no hearing markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress expired.
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas drillers came out ahead: no permit precondition tied to Coast Guard-approved spill plans, no end to categorical exclusions from environmental review, and no extended review deadlines were ever imposed. Coastal communities gained no new statutory protections.

for.name: Rep. C.W. Bill Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to two committees; it was his district's Gulf-adjacent Florida coast that post-Deepwater Horizon rules would protect.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.role: Chair with jurisdiction over the Clean Water Act provisions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for subcommittee or full committee action; after the initial referral to the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee, no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Chair with jurisdiction over the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act provisions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for subcommittee or full committee action; after referral to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, no hearing or markup was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so the partisan shape can only be guessed at from a lone Republican sponsor and committee inaction.

industries.note: The bill would add a Coast Guard-approved spill plan as a permit precondition, end categorical exclusions from environmental review, and lengthen plan review from 30 to as much as 150 days. Its interest in faster, lighter permitting runs against the coastal protection ordinary residents want.
These industries absorb the economic damage when a well blowout closes fisheries and beaches, as the 2010 spill showed. Stronger spill planning and response requirements protect their resource base.
